exchange_medium: Cash (Rs. 2/mo), meals, wool, 2-4 sheep/100 dividend
coding_rationale: Explicit contractual wage shepherding within transhumant pastoralism; dependency of small flock owners on hired labour.
original_excerpt: Malundi or owner of the mal is a shepherd who tends his own flock. But if someone is hired to look after the flock on wages, he is called a pohal... The pohals, when hired, are given (1) free meals, (2) free clothing and wool for the family, (3) two or four sheep per hundred sheep and goats and (4) Rs. 2/- in cash per month as wages.

exchange_medium: Lactation yield (drop from 9 to 4 seers)
coding_rationale: Definitive ecological constraint: alpine frost induces physiological lactation collapse, enforcing sheep/goat specialization.
original_excerpt: No one keeps a buffalo as the climate is not conducive to the proper rearing of buffalo. Once a villager brought a buffalo, but he was not happy with the experience as the milk yield suddenly dropped from 9 srs. to 4 srs. and the buffalo had to be taken to low hills before winter.

exchange_medium: Cash per tola, scrap silver retention, wedding feast gifts
coding_rationale: Artisanal metal craftsmanship converting pastoral livestock profits into portable silver dowry ornaments.
original_excerpt: It is interesting to note that all the three blacksmiths and 2 silversmiths are Sipis and Reharas respectively. It will also be worthwhile to mention that the above table indicates only the primary occupations of the villagers, and instances are not lacking when a man with agriculture as his primary occupation has sheep and goats rearing as his subsidiary occupation.

exchange_medium: Raw wool shares, meals, grain perquisites
coding_rationale: Lower-caste technical monopoly over shearing (katar), weaving tweed (pattu), and tailoring the traditional Gaddi dress (chola/dora).
original_excerpt: The Sipis are the traditional weavers and tailors of the Gaddis. They wash the wool, spin it into yarn and weave the pattu and gardu blankets, and stitch the chola and dora.

exchange_medium: Ghardi (sacrificial sheep neck), sanctified feast food
coding_rationale: Ritual redistribution during Nawala feast crossing purity barriers; Sipi sacred entitlement to sacrificed animal portion.
original_excerpt: At the Shiva Nawala, the priest is usually a Brahman, but the Sipi acts as the traditional musician and drummer (dholak player) and receives the neck portion of the sacrificed sheep and grain.

page_section: p. 11, Society (Brahmin Apex and Land Inducements)
primary_actors: Landed Brahmins & Shakti Devi Temple Shrine
exchange_medium: Royal land endowments (shasan grants) from Raja Meru-Varman
coding_rationale: Historical institutional origin of Brahmin landed monopoly (77% pop) in Chitrari basin.
original_excerpt: The Brahmins occupy the apex of the pyramid representing the caste hierarchy... Rajputs, the original founders of Chamba State, felt that without the Brahmin priests it could not be possible for them to perform religious rites. They invited them from the low-lying areas and offered inducements in the form of giving lands. Most of them entered the State during the period of Meru-Varman who constructed a large number of temples.

exchange_medium: Tied crop-shares, maintenance grain, ploughing labour
coding_rationale: High-caste plough taboos enforcing reliance on attached Halis; contestation of untouchability via Arya Samaj mobility.
original_excerpt: The dominance of one caste group led to the subordinate castes practically depending upon them... Aryas and Halis live aloof. Halis are the traditional ploughmen who cultivate land for the Brahmins under customary arrangements, but have adopted the Arya Samaj name to improve status.

page_section: p. 45, Economy (Rainy Season Gujjar Milk Trade)
primary_actors: Chitrari Hindu Villagers & Visiting Muslim Gujjars
exchange_medium: Cash purchase or cereal barter for high-fat milk/butter on high dhars
coding_rationale: Inter-community trade during monsoon; local cattle produce negligible milk, forcing dependence on mobile pastoralists.
original_excerpt: Milk, therefore, does not form part of their daily diet and is practically non-existent. Even for the purpose of tea, powder milk is to be used. But during the rainy season the Gujjars (a nomadic tribe dealing with milk and its products) come in the nearby areas and settle on the dhars and from there the milk can however, be purchased.

exchange_medium: Customary annual grain collections & temple endowment stipends
coding_rationale: Institutionalized hereditary service caste attached to village temple cult.
original_excerpt: Bensis—This is the smaller caste and is traditionally engaged in playing music and pipes at temples and festive occasions, receiving customary dues from the villagers.

exchange_medium: Dispersed kothas in forest hamlets vs nucleated village core
coding_rationale: Spatial settlement segregation reflecting distinct production strategies: forest cattle-keeping vs nucleated terraced arable.
original_excerpt: The houses are scattered over the mohal in 13 hamlets. Except Maingal hamlet which has 7 houses closely built, other hamlets consist of one or two houses only. Maingal inhabited by Brahmins is surrounded by Gujjar hamlets on three sides... Gujjars do not have separate cattle sheds. Their kothas are divided internally.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Lohar Ironwork and Khalian Remuneration)
exchange_medium: Khalian (customary unhusked grain sheaves from threshing floor)
coding_rationale: Definitive proof of non-monetary jajmani tool maintenance operating in Chamba.
original_excerpt: The Lohar households repair the iron agricultural implements for cultivators. They do not charge cash fees but receive customary shares of unhusked grain (khalian) directly from the threshing floors at each harvest.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Gujjar Buffalo Dairying and Ghee Trade)
primary_actors: Muslim Gujjars & Chamba Town Bazaar Merchants
exchange_medium: Cash currency and credit advances for clarified butter (ghee)
coding_rationale: Commoditization of pastoral surplus linking remote forest hamlets to urban market networks.
original_excerpt: All Gujjar households possess buffaloes. Castewise livestock statistics show that in 25 Gujjar households the number of buffaloes is 217... They sell milk locally and convert surplus into clarified butter (ghee) which is carried down to the Chamba town bazaar for sale.

exchange_medium: Shared water points, bullock loans, dung manure exchange
coding_rationale: Peaceful multi-religious co-existence anchored in complementary non-competing ecological niches.
original_excerpt: Muslim Gujjars are the converts from Hindus. But now they have become devout Muslims and practise Islamic customs. It is due to passage of time that they have slowly imbibed the Islamic way of life, yet live in peace with Hindu neighbours.

exchange_medium: Administrative categorization
coding_rationale: Early colonial racial boundary-making separating Gaddi pastoral core from menial service castes (Sipis, Halis).
original_excerpt: The term 'Gadi' is a generic name, and under this appellation are included Brahmins, Khatris, and a few Rajputs and Rathis... Impure castes are not styled Gadis, but are known by the names of Badi, Sipi, Hali, &c. They are a semi-pastoral, semi-agricultural race. The greater portion of their wealth consists of flocks of sheep and goats.

exchange_medium: Pasture grazing dues (tirni) & British land revenue
coding_rationale: Trans-Dhaula Dhar bi-regional landholding navigating overlapping political borders.
original_excerpt: Many Gadis cultivate the winter crops or wheat in Kangra, and returning with their flocks grow the summer or rain crop at 'Barmor,' as the province on the other side of the snow is designated... They hold lands on this side and also in Chamba, and in former days were considered subject to both States.

exchange_medium: Vernacular folklore
coding_rationale: Proverb capturing environmental precariousness and migratory hardship of high-altitude pastoralism.
original_excerpt: In no-man's-land one makes friends with Gujars and Gaddis.

primary_actors: H. A. Rose & Colonial Ethnographic Taxonomy
exchange_medium: Colonial glossary classification
coding_rationale: Codification of fourfold Gaddi caste taxonomy and migration myths of Mughal flight.
original_excerpt: The Gaddis are divided into four classes: (i) Brahmans, (ii) Khatris and Rajputs who regularly wear the sacred thread, (iii) Thakurs and Rathis who usually do not wear it, and (iv) a menial or dependant class, comprising Kolis, Riharas, Lohars, Badhis, Sipi and Halis, to whom the title of Gaddi is incorrectly applied by outsiders as inhabitants of the Gaderan, though the true Gaddis do not acknowledge them as Gaddis at all.

primary_actors: H. A. Rose & Sipi Service Caste
exchange_medium: Ethnographic ranking
coding_rationale: Documentation of Sipi weaving monopoly combined with subordinate caste positioning.
original_excerpt: Sipi,—The weaver of the Gaddi tribes; found in the Barmaur wizarat of the Chamba State, and virtually the same as the Hali. A low hill-caste who are professional sheep-shearers.

exchange_medium: Pejorative proverbs & administrative stereotypes
coding_rationale: Colonial criminalization of pastoralists reflecting settled revenue bias against mobile graziers.
original_excerpt: When all other castes are dead make friends with a Gujar... But he is far inferior in both personal character and repute to the Jat. He is lazy to a degree, and a wretched cultivator... while his fondness for cattle extends to those of other people.

page_section: p. 112, Sub Table X, Chamba Summary
primary_actors: Khan Ahmad Hasan Khan (1931 Census) & Chamba Population
exchange_medium: Statistical dependency enumeration
coding_rationale: Transition from caste to economic dependency classes (Earners/Dependents) under Great Depression.
original_excerpt: Chamba State: Occupied houses 30,665; Population 146,870; Persons per house 4.79. Rural population overwhelmingly concentrated in small mountainous hamlets.
